speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: Many countries are home-shoring key industries and companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: The competition for investment is fiercer than ever before.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: At the same time, global tax and tariff rules continue to evolve, creating uncertainty and complicating companies' decisions on when and where to invest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: For Singapore to continue to be a choice location for businesses to expand and invest, we must keep our tax system up-to-date, responsive to industry needs and aligned with global tax developments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: First, the amendments to the Multinational Enterprise (Minimum Tax) Act incorporate updates to the Pillar Two rules under the international Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) 2.0 initiative.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: Second, the Bill also brings into legal effect several tax measures already announced in this year's Budget Statement, as well as other changes to our tax system, following close consultations with the industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: I will now briefly outline the amendments to the Multinational Enterprise (Minimum Tax) Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: Last year, Parliament approved the enactment of the Act to implement the Domestic Top-up Tax and the Multinational Enterprise Top-up Tax under the Pillar Two rules.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: Our implementation of the Pillar Two rules is aligned with the global implementation of these rules.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: Major economies, such as the European Union (EU), the United Kingdom (UK) and Japan have already implemented them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: Since the enactment of the Act, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) Inclusive Framework has published new technical clarifications on the Pillar Two rules.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: Clauses 56 to 70 of the Bill will incorporate these and other technical clarifications into our legislation, so that our regime remains up-to-date and consistent and is recognised by other jurisdictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: This will provide certainty to businesses, ease their compliance burdens and most importantly, relieve them from having to pay Pillar Two taxes elsewhere in respect of their Singapore operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: Negotiations on the parameters of Pillar Two have re-opened following the June 2025 G7 statement on the development of a "side-by-side" system that will exempt United States (US)-parented multinational enterprises from specific Pillar Two rules.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: At this point, discussions at the OECD Inclusive Framework are ongoing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: It is unclear what the final outcome will be, and how other jurisdictions and affected businesses will respond.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: For the moment, our considerations for the implementation of the Domestic Top-up Tax and Multinational Enterprise Top-up Tax remain valid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: We are, therefore, proceeding with the implementation of Pillar Two taxes, so that we do not cede tax revenues to other Pillar Two-implementing jurisdictions, and at the same time, we provide tax certainty for multinational enterprises to plan their investments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: We will continue to monitor global developments and if necessary, review this approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: The corporate income tax amendments ensure that our tax system remains responsive to business needs and practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: This is in response to feedback from businesses for more support in their sustainability journeys.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: Currently, tax deductions are only available when certificates or credits are surrendered or retired to meet statutory requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: But with this amendment, tax deductions will now also apply if these certificates or credits are used to meet sustainability commitments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: Clauses 27, 34 and 42 introduce tax incentives recommended by the Equities Market Review Group, set out at Budget this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: These incentives aim to encourage new listings in Singapore's equities market and increase investment demand for Singapore-listed equities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: First, companies that complete a primary or secondary listing with shares offered in conjunction with the listing will enjoy a 20% or 10% Listing Corporate Income Tax Rebate, respectively, subject to caps.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: Second, we will also introduce a 5% concessionary tax rate on qualifying income for new fund manager listings in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: And third, we will introduce a tax exemption on fund managers' qualifying income from funds with at least 30% allocation to Singapore-listed equities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: Moving on to personal income tax, the amendments relate mainly to changes that provide stronger support to our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow) (for the Second Minister for Finance)
text: This was announced in Budget 2025 as part of the SG60 package and is granted automatically to eligible taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While the Bill may appear technical, its implications are wide-ranging.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It keeps Singapore's tax system fair, forward-looking and aligned with global developments and it affects the daily lives of our families, small businesses and workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For individuals, this rebate will especially benefit lower- and middle-income households.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, may I ask how many Singaporeans are expected to face zero income tax liability this year, and how much less personal income tax revenue the Government expects to collect overall?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the longer term, could the Ministry study whether the lowest income tax brackets might also be reduced?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We can make our system more progressive not only by raising rates at the top, but by easing them at the bottom if fiscal space permits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Small enterprises often lack dedicated accounting staff and self-employed workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our freelancers, drivers, tutors and hawkers manage their own filing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While this may appear to be a procedural exercise to give legal effect to the Budget measures, I see it also as an opportunity to do much more.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is an opportunity to refine our tax system so that it continues to work well for Singaporeans and to ensure that our broader national objectives are met, particularly given the critical redistributive role that taxes play in fiscal policy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is also an opportunity to look ahead to make constructive suggestions for the upcoming Budget 2026.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have emphasised in my past Budget speeches, we must move beyond transitional cost of living measures and strengthen structural support through lasting tax changes that achieve greater redistributive efficiency.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As we look towards Budget 2026, how can our tax system best serve Singaporeans, especially at a time of persistent cost pressures and growing inequality?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How can our fiscal architecture reinforce fairness, resilience and growth?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Can our tax policies play a stronger role in redistribution, support for families and domestic capital formation?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I will focus my remarks on three themes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: First, the importance of putting in place structural changes rather than relying on recurring one-off measures.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, the potential role of refundable tax credits in improving equity and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And third, how we can better align our tax system with our ambition to strengthen Singapore's equities market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our tax system should automatically adjust to reflect the economic reality Singaporeans face rather than depending on annual ad hoc adjustments that create uncertainty and administrative complexity.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is similar to the rebate in YA 2024, where it was 50% of tax payable, but capped at $200, and also to the one granted in YA 2019.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Should such rebates become a recurring feature of every budget, they would effectively raise the tax-free threshold for the current $20,000 of chargeable income.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But the Government has framed this as part of the SG60 package, which would suggest that this is only temporary.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Instead of offering periodic rebates, I believe we would be better off instituting a mechanism to regularly review both the personal income tax brackets and basic relief quota to avoid bracket creep, so that the system keeps pace with changes in wages and price over time.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This was a point I had raised in my Parliamentary Question in 2022 and again, in last year's Budget debate.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For workers below 55 years of age, this relief has remained at $1,000 for as long as I can recall.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For older workers aged 55 to 59, the relief stands at $6,000.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And for those aged 60 and above, $8,000.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These figures have not been revised since Budget 2012, more than a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For handicapped workers, the reliefs are also unchanged.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Given the rise in the cost of living, wages and labour participation since then, it is long overdue for a comprehensive update.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In addition, I agree with the exemption from tax of a wide range of initiatives, such as Workfare Training Support Training Allowance, SkillsFuture Mid-Career Training Allowance and Workfare Skill Support.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Again, in the spirit of making scheme-specific changes each time, it would be better for us to introduce a broad-based skills investment relief allowing individuals to claim a capped deduction for out-of-pocket training expenses, and this would be an expansion of the existing course fees relief, which only provides relief for specific approved academic, professional or vocational qualification, or courses relevant to a person's current employment, trade, business, profession or vocation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But at the same time, it does not reward initiatives to better position oneself for an alternative career especially in the current era of rapid change and disruption, as it has no linkages to his or her current profession.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This continues a familiar pattern of annual corporate rebates, varying from 20% to 50% over the last decade, with caps ranging from $10,000 to $40,000.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While such rebates can provide short-term relief, they do not offer the long-term certainty and predictability that businesses, especially SMEs, do require.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I argued in my speech on the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill in 2021, I suggested that we consider introducing more structural progressivity in our corporate income tax regime, particularly to better support local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even as other forms of enterprise support are strengthened, the Government could consider raising partial tax exemption limits or introducing two-tiered corporate profit tax system, similar to Hong Kong's model introduced in 2018.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Such an approach could offer greater certainty than the current system of fluctuating rebates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To illustrate, an SME earning $300,000 in chargeable income today pays around $34,000 in corporate income tax before rebates, an effective tax rate of roughly 11%, compared to about 8% before the exemption restrictions introduced in Budget 2018.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Building these reforms directly into the tax regime, rather than relying on discretionary rebates would send a clearer signal of support to our local enterprise base.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These function as a form of negative income tax, providing benefits through the tax system, but paying out the difference in cash to those with insufficient tax liability to benefit otherwise.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In doing so, they allow the Government to extend supports to lower and middle-income households more efficiently without distorting work incentives or relying on other specific schemes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Refundable credits are widely used in advanced economies, such as the US' Earned Income Tax Credit and Canada's various Refundable Credit Systems, for example.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, one promising area to consider refundable tax credits is in relation to child relief or the Working Mother's Child Relief (WMCR).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While this change benefits some lower-income mothers marginally, my estimate suggests that roughly 80% of working mothers will either be unaffected or worse off with the formula change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have spoken previously about how Singapore's total fertility rate, which fell below 1.0 in 2023 and remained there in 2024, represents an existential challenge.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: President Thaman has pledged that this term of Government will do more to help parents better manage their work and family commitments and to foster a culture that celebrates families.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In that spirit, we should consider whether the revised WMCR structure truly achieves its intent of encouraging married women to stay in the workforce or whether it inadvertently discourages some from doing so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I acknowledge that the Government has said that when the WMCR changes are considered alongside the one-off $2,000 increase in the Child Development Account First Step Grant, about 97% of mothers will be no worse off in the year of birth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But I would also ask what about the next 15 years of tax assessments?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps a reversion of WMCR or its reform into a refundable tax credit could be explored as part of future Budget changes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, this concept is not new to Singapore, with the refundable investment credits already introduced.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My colleague and Member of Parliament for Aljunied group representation constituency (GRC), Mr Kenneth Tiong, will be elaborating further on this point.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Clause 54 operationalises the 13O and 13U Fund Tax Incentive schemes for family offices.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The schemes aim to offer a conducive operating environment for Singapore-based fund managers and family offices.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In my earlier Parliamentary Question in 2022, I had asked about the number of family offices, their aggregate business spending, assets under management (AUM) and local investments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Back then, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) shared that it does not have estimates on aggregate business spending, aggregate AUM help and the amount invested locally by Singapore Family Offices (SFOs).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Otherwise, how do we assess the effectiveness of the capital deployment requirement rules?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even an investment into a global fund distributed by a financial institution with a Singapore presence can qualify.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Greater transparency and periodic reporting of aggregate investment data will also help the public to assess whether these generous tax incentives are delivering tangible benefits to Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, we should consider introducing refundable tax credits to make our fiscal system more equitable and efficient, particularly, in supporting working families and working mothers and lower-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And third, we must align our tax incentives more strategically with our goal of strengthening Singapore's capital markets and ensuring that incentives like those for family offices deliver meaningful local benefits.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Ultimately, our tax system is more than a means of raising revenue.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It reflects our values as a society – fairness, resilience and solidarity.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As we look ahead to Budget 2026, I hope we can take this opportunity to refine our fiscal architecture to serve Singaporeans better, strengthen inclusivity and build an economy that works for all.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The Bill makes several changes to legislation, including to provide for the changes already announced at the landmark Budget 2025.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We should not underestimate the impact that the global minimum tax rules may have on our collective future.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: There are two areas that I will share on.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: First, the impact on Singapore's competitiveness, to be able to attract future foreign investments and create good jobs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And second, the impact on the Government's future revenue collections to support its policy agenda.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: On competitiveness, I believe we will very likely be worse off.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I spent two years at the Economic Development Board.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Tax incentives were a major way to attract multinational enterprises to invest in us, despite our higher labour and land costs, and our smaller market.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It will be like fighting with not one, but both hands tied behind our back and perhaps, with our legs tied together, too.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: How can we start preparing for this new future, and what new tools and value propositions can we create, so that we remain an attractive investment destination?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The Refundable Investment Credit (RIC), is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But in my view, the RIC is helpful; alone it will be insufficient.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Because its benefits, as I understand it, do not scale with an enterprise's growing profits, unlike tax incentives.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: That said, we should not sell ourselves short.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Tax incentives are not the only reason why multinational enterprises come here and create jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We have a clear and established rule of law.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We have good global connectivity from a physical and digital perspective.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And we have an ecosystem of local and global talent that is sticky, because it has been developed over time and our city can provide a high quality of life.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I, therefore, urge the Government to be relentless in developing new value propositions for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This includes investing ahead of demand in world-class industrial infrastructure that could support the faster deployment of high-tech manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It includes making other factors of production more competitive, for example, through investments that make clean or green energy more affordable, more available and more resilient.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It also includes a deepening innovation ecosystem, as well as a preferred base for a reasonable number of global talents that can value-add to our economy and grow our local talent base.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: In short, if the most sophisticated and high-value products can be invented and made only in a few places in the world, Singapore must be one of them.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We will then be able to transcend cost competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time and this is something I feel very strongly about, and I continue to champion strongly for: we should do more to support and grow our local companies because these companies will be more rooted to Singapore even as our cost disadvantages become more apparent.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: With such value propositions, multinational enterprises would be happy to pay these global minimum taxes in Singapore and be rooted here to provide good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Allow me to move on to my second point.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government will need to think harder about the impact on our fiscal system, especially on its revenues.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Many issues are debated in this Parliament Chamber.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Almost all colleagues, including myself, are asking the Government to do more and to spend more, almost never to do less.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: To support its agenda, the Government needs to be on a solid fiscal footing so that its revenues can support its expenditures.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: In terms of Government revenues, we do not yet know how the global minimum tax system will affect us.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: On the one hand, some enterprises will pay more tax.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: On its own, this will lead to more revenues, at least, in the short term.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But on the other hand, enterprises may also choose to pay tax in other jurisdictions or move out of Singapore entirely.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And then, the Government's revenues will be lower.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: No one knows the net fiscal impact and the world is not waiting for us to make an assessment.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: New pronouncements come up from time to time.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The Senior Minister of State for Finance spoke about it, like the "side-by-side" framework between Pillar Two rules and the US tax system.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: MOF echoed this uncertainty in their reply to my Parliamentary Question last month.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I would submit, however, that we will not get greater clarity on our Government's projected revenues anytime soon and this is reasonable.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But the less we know, the more we need to prepare.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And I believe we can adopt a fiscal strategy that provides for different fiscal futures.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: By default, we should be fiscally conservative so that if corporate income tax revenues are low, we would still have enough for our expenditure, especially on our expanding social programmes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But should there be unexpected upsides in corporate income tax revenues, we should think of a structure to share this systematically with all Singaporeans, both in current and in future generations.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: These are but some ideas that can be developed further in time to come, perhaps, at future Budget debates.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And for now, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It provides time-limited tax incentives for both primary and secondary listings.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Before I begin, let me preface by saying I will use the term SGX as shorthand for SGX's equities business.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: SGX, as a whole, is a multi-asset exchange that has great strengths in foreign exchange (FX), commodities and other derivatives.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I think those parts of the business, including BidFX and Iron Ore, have been doing a good job.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: On section 92K, my overall view is that these measures, a time-limited experiment in tax incentives, are in themselves unlikely to move the needle on improving the SGX's competitiveness, for good or bad.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Although I have some general reservations about some of the Bill's principles, on balance, since it is tightly scoped by being both limited in time and capped in subsidy, I support the Bill to give this Government latitude to experiment.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Section 92K introduces a tax rebate to encourage companies to list their shares on SGX.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Shares must be offered to the public in conjunction with the listing.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The company must remain listed throughout the entire five-year period and must apply for approval by 31 December 2027.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The principles on 92K which I have reservations about are: First, the extension of rebates toward secondary listings.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: From the company's perspective, academic research shows secondary listings work primarily when listing in the US, where companies gain from purported superior governance standards or valuation premiums.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is debatable if Singapore offers either advantage.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The advantages are not of secondary listings in general but of the US in particular.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I can understand why SGX might want to encourage secondary listings.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This was dwarfed by secondary offerings, which was a hundred times larger at $4.3 billion.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: SGX's function as a capital raising venue for already listed companies is currently much more significant than its listings.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: SGX Chairman Koh Boon Hwee, has argued for the need to take calculated first-mover risks to build liquidity.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Presumably anchoring more secondary listings is one of those first-mover risks.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But from Singapore's perspective, I do not see much benefit in giving incentives to attract secondary listings, especially combined with a disclosure-based regime, which may result in a bigger slate of lower quality companies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: At the point of entry, many may just make the number of listings and market cap look better, while not creating broad local employment since their operations are overseas.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Some may disagree on the basis that these secondary listings may improve liquidity and generate turnover.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But how much of this is sticky, multi-year liquidity, and how much is transient event-driven volume?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I ask: what is the basis of the Government's belief that it will lead to high-quality liquidity?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For me, the bigger philosophical questions from first principles – why would a company want to do a secondary listing in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Why would Singapore benefit overall from more secondary listings in a disclosure-based regime? – remain inadequately answered.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Overall, I would rather we focus on attracting quality primary listings over extending incentives to secondary listings.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But since the trial is limited in time and scope, we will support the Bill scope in toto.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We hope the results will be published and guide future market development.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Bill addresses three key technical problems regarding secondary listings.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Many secondary listings come by introduction, meaning no new shares sold, which leaves little local free float and tends to depress local turnover.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Hong Kong Exchange (HKEX) warns that secondary listings can suffer from failure to develop or sustain an active trading market, which is why they flag such stocks prominently with an "S" marker.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Multiple high-profile SGX secondary listings were by way of introductions, meaning no new shares.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This includes a 2010 listing of Prudential and the 2022 SGX listing of electric vehicle company, Nio Inc, which GIC is now suing for securities fraud in the Southern District of New York.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: These secondaries have had thin local trading versus their primary venues, with exception of the Jardine Group.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So far, secondary listings have been a mixed bag.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I will return to this point about poor quality listings later.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But technically, 92K insists that shares must be offered to the public, ensuring some float, so listings by introduction are excluded from rebates.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And while this is not in the Bill, I note that MAS has the Grant for Equity Market Singapore (GEMS) Research Development Grant, which provides a top-up per research report, more if it covers pre-Initial Public Offering and newly-listed names.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This will help strengthen the value proposition of a listing here in Singapore, even if we cannot offer much valuation premium.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The tax rebates are also tied to the profitability of the company.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If the companies are loss-making, they will not qualify for the rebates.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If it were not the case, we could be attracting rebate tourism from dubious companies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The second principle I have reservations on is this whole idea of giving listing incentives at all.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I could not find much evidence that having listing incentives will improve the quality of companies or long-term performance.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the converse was more likely true.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Quebec Stock Savings Plan, which offered taxpayers generous tax write-offs for investment in new public stock issues of companies, drove a short-term surge in small company primary issues.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But many issuers later disappeared or posted weaker earnings.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The impact on capitalisation was short-lived and overall, stimulus effects were limited.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For listing incentives, from the company's perspective, it may be unsustainable once incentives end and these companies may fail or simply delist when that time comes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What we are likely to see is a short-term pop in the numbers, because without answers to permanent questions around liquidity disclosure, quality, investor depth and regulatory credibility, strong secular headwinds remain.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Some say it is a chicken-and-egg problem, building liquidity and investor depth.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I understand this view, but I believe that raising the quality of listed companies is pre-conditional to building this two-sided market.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Other jurisdictions are not focusing on financial incentives.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Hong Kong is focused on raising corporate governance standards, enforcement and improving processing efficiency, which is, in my view, a more correct approach.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Hong Kong's listing rules have historically been stricter than SGX in areas such as independence of directors, remuneration disclosures and related party transactions, and their regulators have been much more aggressive in enforcement actions, including against directors.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Hong Kong recently introduced a new Corporate Governance Code with stricter requirements: limiting independent non-executive directors to six listed directorships, mandatory continuing professional training, broad skills matrices and performance reviews.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They are raising standards without using financial incentives.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Removing it does not increase disclosure; it removes a critical warning signal.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Industry players supporting its removal may of course benefit from more trading volume, even if low-quality.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Their incentives may not align with retail investor protection.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I will now move on to a few remarks on the principles that should underlie our stock market.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: At its core, a stock market strikes a "domestic bargain": savers get high-quality asset appreciation and local enterprises get capital and exit opportunities.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: All other functions, such as foreign capital allocating to Singapore, or overseas companies listing in Singapore, are extensions of this core.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: First, the "ASEAN gateway" strategy is becoming obsolete.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It may have worked for Singapore when other Southeast Asian countries did not have a strong local market, but today, Thailand and Vietnam have their own mature and highly liquid markets with domestic brand recognition.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: ASEAN companies no longer have as many compelling reasons to list on the SGX, vis-a-vis their home exchanges.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, our regulatory reach is limited over other foreign markets.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This means for foreign companies, we are exposed to information asymmetry and governance risks we cannot adequately mitigate, such as, for the fraud-accused Nio.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The tidal force of passive investment is a secular supertrend.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Sovereign wealth funds like Norway's leading Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG) have demonstrated that low-cost passive investing outperforms the active management approach.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I believe passive strategies will form the basis of significant portfolio allocations going forward.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But passive investment requires something fundamental, high quality indexes or baskets worth buying.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Investors must be able to trust that the baskets of stocks they are purchasing represent genuine value, not a random collection of mediocre companies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: By lowering listing standards and removing investor protections like the financial watch list, the risk is that the quality of the SGX and Straits Times Index (STI) is allowed to degrade precisely when global capital is demanding higher quality for passive allocation.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Let us not forget that active management, to weed out mediocrity, is an expensive endeavour.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: You will pay an active manager above and beyond to do due diligence to separate weed from chaff, and these active management fees are a drag on any future returns.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: You cannot attract passive capital by diluting the quality of your index.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Any slackening in market shaping and maintaining quality standards cuts directly against one of the most important structural trends in modern finance.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I am bearish on any cutting of standards.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Without quality and coherence, we cannot articulate what our market represents.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Secondary listings like Jardine Matheson and Hongkong Land, both managed from Hong Kong, comprise 5% of the Index, but represent neither Singapore operations nor "Singapore Inc's" core capital-formation interests.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Defensiveness and leakages are headwinds in building a future coherent story to ultimately increase SGX's valuation premium.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What would a future coherent story look like?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Not mimicking NASDAQ's high-beta growth, not remaining purely defensive, but rather a foundation of quality SMEs, profitable, well-run, the "domestic bargain" in action, complemented by selective growth engines from a robust R&D industrial policy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The local stock market is currently dominated by Government-linked Companies (GLCs).

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: However, Singapore has a long tail of well-run profitable SMEs, which do require growth capital.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They are not super growth companies, but they deserve capital and can anchor our index.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We need to meet our economy where it is.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: SMEs are the companies that will benefit most from a supportive exchange ecosystem, including the long-tail of research needed to cover them.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The second layer will be selective growth from R&D.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Commercial offshoots from our Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) masterplans in Pharmaceuticals, Advanced Manufacturing and Deep Tech should be able to list an earlier stage, in order to access domestic capital.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Without opining on the commercial validity of that specific decision, I believe capital intensive R&D ventures could benefit from accessible public markets.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Earlier stage listings would build local investor familiarity with science-based companies and allow incremental capital raising as milestones are met, and would perhaps have improved the odds for some of the first generation Biopolis companies which failed.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That is why I support SGX RegCo's amending of admission requirements for life sciences companies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: With your indulgence, Sir, before I end, as this Bill touches on the stock market, I would like to correct some statements about the Workers' Party (WP) stock market proposals.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Minister Chee Hong Tat, at the DBS hosted a fireside chat on 22 October 2025, said, I quote, "Over the past year, we have worked closely with the industry to come up with proposals that could enhance the liquidity and competitiveness of Singapore's equities markets.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We decided not to go for quick fixes, such as asking GIC or Temasek to pump-prime the market by mandating them to invest a certain amount in local equities.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I explained in Parliament previously, in response to similar calls by the Workers' Party, that I do not believe such superficial measures will be effective and sustainable.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This is what the Chinese call, "治标不治本", solutions that may sound good in theory but actually do not solve the underlying problems facing our equities markets." I am not sure what calls the Minister was referring to.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I have looked around and asked my colleagues, but have drawn a blank.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: My colleague Louis Chua did speak in this year's Committee of Supply about our stock market, but he suggested two things: letting more of Temasek's GLCs list on SGX; and strengthening corporate governance standards.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, respectfully, I would like to ask the Minister to please clarify and source his comments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My colleagues, MP Louis Chua and MP Kenneth Tiong have dealt with the first and second elements of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will confine my reactions to the Multinational Enterprise (Minimum Tax) Act and parts of the Income Tax Act related to multinational enterprises.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I support the Bill, I have a few specific concerns about several legislative elements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will also speak more broadly about what it means to stick to BEPS 2.0 in a Trump 2.0 world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Parts G and H of clause 56 of the Bill, insert subsections that define "securitisation entities" and "securitisation arrangements", established by multinationals to help investors manage insolvency risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Securitised entities and arrangements are ubiquitous in modern enterprise design and operation and I understand that these may have been introduced as a result of public feedback requesting greater clarity on their treatment when it comes to domestic top-up tax calculations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My concern has to do with the role that securitised entities have historically played in modern finance and especially how securitisation allowed financial institutions to carry far riskier portfolios than otherwise possible; which contributed in turn to the 2007/2008 Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is because securitised products, such as the infamous collateralised debt obligations (CDOs), CDO-squared and other forms of asset-backed securities, increased the informational distance between regulators and banks, which then elevated the fragility of the system and set the stage for a full-blown crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While there is little reason to believe that similar securitisation arrangements are inducing the sort of undesirable risk-taking in the context of multinational enterprises' (MNEs') approach to BEPS, it is nevertheless useful to keep in mind the key lesson from that earlier episode that corporations can and do employ securitisation to skirt rules and regulations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, it is important that our authorities be alert to the possibility that MNEs may choose to park otherwise taxable assets in such arrangements and special purpose vehicles, which this legislation explicitly accommodates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In his response at that time, Prime Minister Wong assured the House that "the RIC is compliant with BEPS." Singapore's approach to transfer pricing currently takes strong reference from the OECD's own guidelines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In practice, this requires that intellectual property (IP) to be valued at arms-length, open-market prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Presumably, then, this implies that RICs must likewise conform with transfer pricing of intangible IP, including hard-to-value intangibles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In scrutinising clause 45 of the Bill, however, I did not find any such restrictions written into the language of the proposed legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The requirement for arms' length conditions do, however, appear in the original Income Tax Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: All in this House are undoubtedly aware that we appear to be transitioning from what had hitherto been a robust, US-led, rules-based international economic order, toward one that is much more transactional, where might makes right, and the US – rather than being a global caretaker – comes across instead as an economic bully.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Small countries, such as Singapore, are unavoidably at a disadvantage in such a Machiavellian system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This applies to an international project such as BEPS, which is heavily reliant on the buy-in of nations to sustain it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Does the exit of the US from the system irreparably undermine BEPS and the multinational minimum tax?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is, of course, the fear that many have.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my view, however, the future of international tax rules is likely to unfold in much the same way that the global trading system has been evolving: steadily grinding forward, even in the absence of the US.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, the ability of countries to proceed with top-up taxes, even without the acquiescence or compliance of other countries is largely built into the design of global rules.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Admittedly, unilateral action performed without the cover of a treaty may invite retaliatory responses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is, perhaps, somewhat for fortuitous, since UTPR has been a sore point for the Trump administration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There may yet be room for reconciliation of the disparate positions between US and the rest of the signatories of BEPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another might grant US entities permanent safe harbour instead of just a temporary one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is some text in the Bill, notably on clause 59, that speaks to safe harbours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But only to the extent that it aligns the timing of elections of globe safe harbours with no real mention of their permanence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These considerations have yet to be weaved into the Multinational Enterprise (Minimum Tax) Act, which is, at this point, appropriate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I believe it would be premature to do so, given the volatile nature of the Trump administration's policymaking and the BEPS roll out process, more generally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, that does not preclude us from planning ahead.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I wish to declare that I am the chief executive officer of an investment management company.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These include the Equities Market Review Group recommended tax incentives.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These incentives support our capital markets and can create skilled jobs in analysis, research and compliance – jobs that many young Singaporeans can aspire to.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A key change concerns section 13W of Income Tax Act, which exempts gains on the disposal of ordinary shares.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Separately, preference shares will qualify if accounted for as equity under the investee's standards or under the International Financial Reporting Standards.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, registered business trusts and variable capital companies are not included in this 20% shareholding threshold definition.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As these structures are key to our capital markets ecosystem, I urge the Government to consider extending the definition to registered business trusts and variable capital companies.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Bill also proposes amendments to the Multinational Enterprise (Minimum Tax) Act 2024.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is to align our laws with the OECD's Pillar Two Global Minimum Tax framework.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore has long had a pro-enterprise, relatively low-tax environment, which helps attract good investment, fund management, corporate listings and regional headquarters.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, with the global minimum tax framework, centralising business operations into low-tax jurisdictions will no longer be as straight-forward as before.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With Multinational Enterprise (Minimum Tax) Act, Singapore's adoption of the global 15% minimum tax ensures parity across jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And for Singapore, it gets its fair share of this minimum global tax.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This Bill ensures that our tax base remains defensible while preserving our attractiveness for high-quality investments.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By refining definitions in the Multinational Enterprise (Minimum Tax) Act, we align our fiscal framework with international norms, reinforcing Singapore as a transparent and rules-based jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With global minimum taxes, non-tax competitive advantages become more critical.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, I offer five suggestions: one, issue comprehensive transitional guidelines early and provide simplified tax computation tools or advisory clinics; two, publish a clause-by-clause table of effective dates, listing which provisions are retrospective, prospective or transitional to reduce ambiguity; three, provide transitional or good faith relief, allow self-correction in the next assessment year without penalty for companies that relied on prior law; four, review Pillar Two compliance costs to ensure reporting obligations remain proportionate for multinationals headquartered here; and finally, five, harmonise definitions across tax laws via consolidated glossary, ensuring consistent interpretation across the Income Tax Act, Multinational Enterprise (Minimum Tax) Act and GST Act.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I ask for, first of all, for everybody's understanding that I will not be able to address everybody's suggestions today, and this includes Mr Kenneth Tiong's suggestions on equities market improvements, which are outside the scope of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: In line with the Standing Order 70(2), specifying that the Second Reading should be on the general merits and principle of the Bill, let me first respond to some of the points that are more specific to the Bill that other colleagues have raised.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Victor Lye have asked whether we would adjust our implementation of Pillar Two top-up taxes if other jurisdictions slow or reverse their adoption and whether this would affect our economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The reopening of negotiations on Pillar Two, including the side-by-side solution, seeks to exempt US multinational enterprises from some of the Pillar Two rules has, indeed, created some uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But our key consideration for imposing the Pillar Two taxes, to avoid ceding tax revenue, remains valid for now.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: It is far from clear what the final arrangement will be.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: As Mr Shawn Loh said, the less we know, the more we should prepare.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And so, MOF will continue to monitor developments very closely and recalibrate our approach, if needed, if and when the situation changes.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Mr Louis Chua asked if companies that received the RIC are required to adopt the arm's length principle.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Mr Shawn Loh spoke about the importance of enhancing Singapore's value proposition to global enterprises and let me assure Members that this is a key priority for the Government.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: While Pillar Two may reduce the room for tax competition amongst jurisdictions, the competition for foreign investment has intensified.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The Prime Minister explained during past Budget debates that, although BEPS 2.0 was meant to tilt the playing field in favour of governments and to make MNEs pay more taxes, in reality, such enterprises wield considerable leverage, and this is why governments everywhere are, therefore, still spending significant sums to attract investments.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Fortunately, our economic competitiveness is not based solely on tax incentives, but on the strength of our overall business ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And this includes many factors – a deep pool of human capital, strong rule of law, long-term investments in infrastructure and connectivity, and our capacity to deploy and diffuse new technologies.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I chair one of the committees on global competitiveness with Senior Minister of State Low Yen Ling.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We are developing ideas to strengthen Singapore's value proposition in the global economy to build new growth sectors, such as advanced manufacturing precision medicine and artificial intelligence; to attract fast growing companies from the US, China, India and elsewhere; to strengthen Singapore's position as a global hub in the flows of goods, capital, talent, data, energy and ideas.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The objective, as always, is to secure good growth for Singapore and good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And this is why our tax system will have to complement the strategy too.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: At the company level, we do regularly review the tax system to ensure that it is responsive to industry needs and feedback, and that is why MOF has consulted extensively with SMEs, trade associations and chambers for this Bill.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Facilitating businesses' tax compliance has been, and always will be, a priority for IRAS.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: In this regard, IRAS has been publishing e-tax guides and updating its website to provide clearer guidance for businesses.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: IRAS has also simplified the tax filing processes for small businesses, such as by reducing the amount of information that they need to submit in their tax returns.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Pillar Two rules are complex, and to help taxpayers better understand and comply with these rules, IRAS has also set up a dedicated mailbox and published e-learning videos and an e-tax guide on the top-up taxes for the businesses to refer to.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also asked on the compliance requirement for securitisation entities.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Our approach to the top-up tax on such entities, or how we would impose the top-up tax is similar to the treatment in other jurisdictions, including in Australia and Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: This is to avoid ceding tax revenue to foreign jurisdictions that impose Pillar Two taxes on securitisation entities income.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Mr Saktiandi asked about Singapore's implementation plans for the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: This framework provides for the automatic exchange of information on crypto assets for tax purposes with partner jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Mr Saktiandi further highlighted that the short window of the listing corporate income tax rebate incentive and its administrative requirements could discourage participation, and he asked whether or not as well whether the rebate would be effective given our implementation of Pillar Two taxes.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: While tax measures may be less relevant for large multinational enterprises that are affected by Pillar Two, they will still benefit small businesses or smaller businesses.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Ultimately, it is up to each enterprise to consider its own circumstances before applying for any incentive.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: MOF will monitor the effectiveness of these incentives and we will be open to making further adjustments if necessary.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Mr Chua spoke about how we should review our tax incentives for family officers to strengthen their economic outcomes for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Indeed, this is what Singapore does for all of our incentives on a regular basis, and I agree with him and I thank him for his feedback.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Mr Victor Lye suggested setting a clear timeline to extend the enhancement to the 20%-shareholding condition for section 13W tax exemption of disposal gains to registered business trusts and variable capital companies.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: MOF will indeed study the feasibility of his suggestion, but please give us some time as the ownership structures of registered business trusts and variable capital companies are complex.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: This is because a tax-paying company would be considered an active company, and this approach allows for greater administrative efficiency while still meeting our intent of supporting active companies.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: However, section 92L(5) does give the Government the flexibility to adjust the employment condition if companies are unable to meet it due to unforeseen circumstances.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Indeed, we have shared the upsides of Singapore's economic growth, including through tax rebates with Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Mr Saktiandi and Mr Louis Chua suggested making structural changes to our tax system to provide more support for individuals, such as reducing the rates for the lowest income tax brackets, or to increase the quantum of our tax reliefs.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Mr Chua also suggested reviewing our personal income tax exemption threshold of $20,000.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Our personal income tax exemption threshold is already higher than jurisdictions like Australia and Malaysia, where thresholds range from $1,500 to $16,000.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Taken together with our progressive tax rates, tax reliefs and rebates, already around 40% of workers do not pay income tax in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: For those who do, about 80% have an effective tax rate of less than 6%.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Most lower-wage workers, as I said, do not already pay income tax, but in the event that any worker has paid income tax on the training allowances received, the amendment allows them to obtain a refund of the taxes paid, and this will be publicised by Workforce Singapore, so that such individuals can come forward to do so, Mr Deputy Speaker, in conclusion, as a small open economy, Singapore must remain nimble and responsive to global developments.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Our fundamentals are strong, and we are well placed to seize opportunities amidst the shifts in the global economic environment, this Tax Bill will update our tax regime to provide more clarity to businesses and to respond to industry feedback, and this is a key part of our overall effort to strengthen Singapore's economic competitiveness as the global landscape continues to evolve.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Are there any clarifications for the Senior Minister of State for Finance?
